title: How to define your corporate purpose
summary: A strong corporate purpose gives your whole company a clear north star. Here's how to zero in on your unique values.
body_text: Corporate purpose is the reason a business exists beyond making a profit. A company with a strong corporate purpose sets forth a vision of a better world and commits to helping make that vision into a reality. Purpose is a company’s north star. It guides decision making at every level—from product development to hiring practices and marketing strategies. In particular, an authentic purpose lends credibility to corporate social responsibility (CSR) programs. Authenticity is essential because customers and employees expect businesses have a clear corporate purpose that they actually follow through on. Being authentic means that the ideals you commit to are a natural extension of your business mission. But that commitment isn’t enough. You also need to articulate your purpose in a way that resonates with all stakeholders–employees, customers, your community, and more. A good corporate purpose not only makes an impact, it sets an example for others to follow. If your company doesn’t have an authentic purpose or you aren’t communicating it clearly to all your stakeholders, here’s how to sharpen your vision and message. {{cta}} How to shape your corporate purpose messaging Most companies have everything they need to create a compelling and authentic corporate purpose. But it takes work to bring all the elements together. Step 1: Start with your “why” Corporate purpose is the reason your business exists at all. It connects what you do to why you do it . Again, it’s not just about making a profit. It’s about how your company shapes the world. The concept of purpose is often used interchangeably with vision. But the two are distinct. Purpose often changes over time as the business grows or the culture shifts, while vision can hold steady in the long term. To define your corporate purpose, start with the reason your company exists: As a company, what problem are you solving for your customers? How do your products or services improve people’s lives ? What unique point of view do you bring to the table? What kind of workplace do you aim to create for employees? Starting with these questions will ensure that your corporate purpose stays aligned to your business mission. If you look at CVS Health’s purpose , you can see how it connects to their products and services. Their purpose is to “bring our heart to every moment of your health.” They aim to make people’s lives better through empathy and trust, and they build their teams and processes around that. eBay strives to “make selling and buying equitable and attainable for all.” This purpose is a natural extension of their product, which connects individual buyers and sellers. As they’ve built out their messaging around community programs and business initiatives, they consistently evoke this idea of equity and inclusivity. Step 2: Plant your flag You’ve clarified how you improve your customers’ lives. Now it’s time to connect that to a broader story. You need to define the change your company wants to be in the world . This requires you to identify and commit to a set of values. Values are principles or standards that guide decisions inside the organization. They’re often aspirational, meaningful in a larger context, and consistent with the overall company vision. But values cannot be vague or theoretical. They need to connect to concrete actions. Employees should be able to see the thru-line of how your company’s values impact business initiatives. For some companies, this might be baked into the business mission. For instance, Desolenator , a company that produces thermal desalination technology, can draw a clear line from the innovative product they make to the sustainable and equitable world they aim to create . Other companies might need to do more work to create that thru-line. CarMax is the nation’s largest retailer of used cars. Their purpose is to “drive integrity by being honest and transparent in every action.” That purpose not only shapes how they do business, but also their commitment to a diverse workplace and community investment . Incorporating values into your corporate purpose ensures that the story you craft feels authentic and connects to your company’s roots. Plus, strong values create a sense of meaning for everyone within the company. Ultimately, that’s what defines brand identity and helps to retain talent. Step 3: Weave in your origin story Your origin story matters. And crafting the story of how your company was born is a crucial step in defining a corporate purpose that is genuine and will resonate with others. The path of building a business—from that first lightbulb moment to hiring a team—is an important tale. It’s often a story of struggle, hard lessons learned, and sometimes surprise challenges. Resilience is powerful. What’s more, an origin story reveals people’s creativity and drive. Communicating a business success story humanizes the people behind it: the founders and investors, the board of directors, and the employees. So collect key story elements: the history, what sets the company apart from competitors, and the background of the people leading the way today. Weave this origin story together with the values you’ve identified to create a narrative that resonates on a personal level. Bringing all these elements together ensures your corporate purpose feels like natural evolution for your company. And it keeps the story from falling flat. Dick’s Sporting Goods aims to equip all athletes to achieve their dreams. They tie that purpose to the story of Dick Stack, who started the company with $300 and a relentless work ethic. Connecting their purpose to a personal narrative helps people understand how their corporate purpose is woven into the company’s DNA, making it clear that it’s an authentic commitment, not just a PR play. Make corporate purpose your north star An authentic corporate purpose involves more than crafting a mission statement and then allowing it to collect dust. Corporate purpose should genuinely guide decisions across the entire company over time, whether large or small. Corporate purpose is a way of thinking and operating. It’s a north star, not a press release. While a corporate purpose should feel aspirational, it also needs to be concrete enough for employees to actualize. Every time employees start a new project or initiative, they should make an effort to connect what they’re doing to the corporate purpose. This practice shows the company’s commitment to putting values into action and helps everyone stay connected to the meaning behind their work. Google ‘s corporate purpose statement is a good example: “To organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful.” This is simultaneously a big idea , yet also feels understandable. It provides direction to employees when approaching problems or new projects, guiding them towards the company’s priorities. Jen Carter, global head of technology & volunteering at Google.org At Google, their purpose extends into Google.org, the philanthropic arm of the company. During the Impact Studio Conference , Jen Carter, global head of technology & volunteering at Google.org, explained how she and her team leverage the company’s core ethos in their corporate giving programs: “Google is a place that has a big appetite for risky bets. We call them moonshots. So from Google.org’s earliest days, we’ve really looked for places where we can test out new ideas and direct risk capital toward big problems.” She went on to explain the impetus for the Google.org Fellowship program started by a desire to help fix healthcare.gov's launch. Corporate social responsibility is an extension of corporate purpose Consider corporate purpose a fundamental mindset that keeps the company on the right track. It bears repeating that this is more than a statement on the website. As important as it is for your purpose to shape internal company culture and drive business strategy, it won’t mean much if it stops there. To make your purpose meaningful, you need to engage in corporate social responsibility (CSR). CSR is how you make an impact on the community and help shape the world inside and outside of your company. Corporate purpose should inform your overall CSR strategy, corporate philanthropy programs, and efforts around environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing. If corporate purpose is an identity, action in these areas is how you express it. Without establishing a corporate purpose first, everything related to your CSR will likely lack substance and direction. If you have yet to develop a CSR or corporate philanthropy strategy—or if you are suddenly searching “what’s ESG!?”— we’ve got you . Start by asking these questions: What resources can you leverage to help the local or global community? Can you offer corporate volunteering programs for employees to give back during normal work hours? What kind of giving program can you sponsor? Can you offer corporate matching for charitable donations? How can you form or strengthen partnerships with community organizations? How can you ensure sustainability in your operations? When it comes to CSR, you don’t have to do it all right away. Try different approaches and commit to iterating and growing as you go. Be sure to find a suite of CSR software that can grow with you. Remember, neither your corporate purpose nor your CSR programs are static. They should evolve as needs change and priorities shift. And none of this work happens in a vacuum. It’s all in conversation with the work other companies, nonprofits, community members, and public institutions are doing to make the world a better place.

Atualizações tecnológicas exigem tempo e dinheiro, e como diz o ditado, “Se não está quebrado, não conserte.” Mas há uma linha tênue entre atualizar sua frota de dispositivos móveis cedo demais e atualizá-la tarde demais – e um compromisso de tempo e dinheiro muito maior com o último. Infelizmente, muitas organizações estão começando a estender a vida útil de seus dispositivos demais e introduzindo riscos significativos em seus negócios. O seu é um deles? Bem, se sua organização ainda estiver usando… Dispositivos Android 8 ou mais antigos, então você pode ter perdido o suporte de segurança. Isso significa que informações confidenciais sobre seus clientes, funcionários, parceiros e toda a operação podem ser facilmente expostas se alguém perceber que suas defesas estão baixas. Dispositivos com Android 11 e mais antigos, então você pode já ter perdido a capacidade de usar novos aplicativos disponíveis na Google Play Store. Isso é um problema para TI, gerentes, trabalhadores da linha de frente e qualquer pessoa que precise da ajuda de aplicativos mais novos para fazer seu trabalho. Os dispositivos Zebra que funcionam com os chipsets Qualcomm 8937 (SD430) tiveram o suporte do fabricante encerrado em janeiro de 2024. Isso significa que você não tem como obter correções de segurança para ameaças críticas ou de alto risco ou vulnerabilidades recém-identificadas. Se alguma das situações acima se aplica a você, você precisa substituir seus dispositivos por outros mais novos imediatamente. Eu sei que isso é frustrante. O próprio dispositivo pode parecer novo em folha. Mas há muita coisa que entra em jogo para fazer um dispositivo funcionar da maneira que você precisa, incluindo o software. Se você continuar usando dispositivos mais antigos, não poderá mais fazer as atualizações de recursos de segurança e desempenho necessárias para manter seus dados seguros e suas equipes produtivas no clima de negócios de hoje. Como sei que você pode precisar convencer seu chefe (ou outros aprovadores de compra/orçamento) a gastar dinheiro em novos dispositivos e possivelmente em algum desenvolvimento de software, vamos falar sobre todas as funcionalidades que você/sua organização perde – e os riscos que você herda – se tentar fazer seus dispositivos móveis mais antigos funcionarem por mais. Vulnerabilidades de segurança de dados não serão a única coisa que causará dores de cabeça se você continuar usando esses dispositivos. O que acontece quando um dispositivo móvel envelhece Antes de prosseguir, quero reconhecer que provavelmente parece estranho que eu esteja recomendando que você substitua dispositivos móveis que são construídos para durar anos e são elogiados por sua extrema durabilidade. E, sim, se você está dando a cada um de seus funcionários de linha de frente um dispositivo móvel robusto, projetado especificamente para o ambiente e aplicação em que são usados todos os dias (ou seja, acompanhamento de processos de trabalho em uma linha de produção, recebimento de mercadorias, entregas de encomendas, cuidados com pacientes ou resposta a emergências), então o próprio dispositivo – o hardware – provavelmente pode durar uma década ou mais. Esses tipos de dispositivos são construídos para sobreviver a qualquer coisa, então eles podem nunca experimentar o tipo de dano físico que é comum em dispositivos de consumo e justifica a substituição frequente do dispositivo. No entanto, há uma tonelada de componentes internos que estão envelhecendo muito mais rápido do que o exterior do dispositivo pode parecer, então você não pode avaliar a viabilidade contínua de um dispositivo com base em quão bom ele ainda parece. O chipset e o sistema operacional (OS) que alimentam o dispositivo, a tecnologia wireless que o conecta a redes e outros dispositivos, e o software e as ferramentas de segurança que o executam vão se tornar obsoletos antes do próprio dispositivo. Eles podem ser viáveis apenas por 3–5 anos devido às atuais demandas de segurança da informação, requisitos de desempenho ou ofertas de suporte do fabricante e do provedor do sistema operacional – e, infelizmente, não podem ser substituídos/consertados quando começam a falhar. Não podemos entrar e substituir ou reparar certos componentes ou sistemas à medida que envelhecem. Nem podemos desacelerar o envelhecimento. Quando o chipset, o sistema operacional, as tecnologias wireless e outros componentes atingem o fim da vida útil, o mesmo acontece com o dispositivo em si. Portanto, se um computador móvel portátil, wearable ou tablet só for viável até o Android 11, por exemplo, e você precisar usar um aplicativo que só está disponível em dispositivos que executam o Android 13 ou mais recente, então você não terá escolha a não ser atualizar seu dispositivo ou abrir mão do uso desse aplicativo. Você poderia se adaptar? Você poderia encontrar uma solução alternativa? Talvez parar de usar esse aplicativo por um tempo? Claro. Mas a que custo? Quais são as implicações para o negócio? Quais são os riscos que você aceita quando espera um pouco mais para atualizar seus dispositivos e fazer com que seus aplicativos de negócios funcionem de forma otimizada? E quando um pouco mais se transforma em muito tempo? Bem, posso colocá-lo em contato com alguns líderes empresariais que, infelizmente, descobriram isso na prática. Apenas recentemente, o Google enviou uma atualização para os Play Services que revelou um problema oculto em versões mais antigas do sistema operacional Android A atualização tornou os dispositivos inutilizáveis. O problema foi resolvido em versões mais recentes do sistema operacional Android há vários anos, mas organizações que ainda usavam dispositivos/versões do sistema operacional mais antigas para gerenciar operações diárias eram vulneráveis à falha. Eles perderam vários dias de produtividade enquanto a Zebra os ajudava a corrigir o problema – embora a "correção" fosse apenas para esse problema, não para todos os outros que os dispositivos mais antigos estavam apresentando ou poderiam causar no futuro. Eu sei que muitas vezes na vida – e nos negócios – queremos esticar nossos recursos o máximo possível. Ninguém quer ser desperdiçador. Mas usar tecnologia antiga pode ser ainda mais desperdiçador do ponto de vista material e financeiro. Isso também desperdiça muito tempo dos profissionais de TI e da linha de frente, pois eles estão frequentemente distraídos tentando solucionar problemas ou contornar problemas que surgem com a tecnologia mais antiga. O que exige uma atualização do dispositivo Se você quer saber com certeza quando é hora de atualizar sua frota de dispositivos móveis, considere estas quatro coisas: 1. Segurança – No momento em que você perde o suporte de segurança do fornecedor do sistema operacional ou do fabricante do dispositivo, é hora de atualizar. Aguardar até mesmo um dia após a data de "fim do suporte" deixa sua empresa, clientes e parceiros vulneráveis a exposições de dados sensíveis porque, como mencionei anteriormente, você não poderá mais acessar os serviços que fornecem atualizações de segurança de rotina ou correções para vulnerabilidades críticas, de alto risco e recém-descobertas. Você se tornará essencialmente um alvo fácil toda vez que esse dispositivo mais antigo for usado. Por outro lado, assim que você colocar um novo dispositivo nas mãos dos seus trabalhadores de linha de frente, você terá acesso total a serviços que monitoram vulnerabilidades e enviam automaticamente correções de segurança e software atualizado para seus dispositivos. Se você estiver usando dispositivos da Zebra, terá proteção 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana, através do Lifeguard e suporte adicional através do Zebra OneCare durante o período de suporte. Os dispositivos mais novos não apenas fornecem atualizações regulares de segurança, mas também possuem novos recursos de segurança que protegem ainda mais os dispositivos. Por exemplo, novos dispositivos suportam uma criptografia de arquivos mais segura – ou seja, File Based Encryption (FBE) – e vêm com o Secure Boot padrão que garante que o sistema operacional não foi comprometido. Novamente, essas não são coisas que você pode adicionar retroativamente a dispositivos mais antigos para atualizá-los aos padrões modernos de segurança e desempenho. 2. Compatibilidade de aplicativos – Se os riscos de segurança de "esperar mais" para substituir seus dispositivos não são motivação suficiente, ou você acha que pode encontrar suporte de outras maneiras, saiba que o Google está traçando um limite quando se trata de compatibilidade de aplicativos, exigindo que novos aplicativos na Play Store devem ter como alvo o Nível de API 13 (Android 13) ou superior. Isso limitará a disponibilidade de aplicativos disponíveis para você para dispositivos mais antigos, o que pode prejudicar sua capacidade de melhorar a eficiência operacional e os resultados do negócio. 3. O impacto de velocidades e feeds nos resultados do negócio – Seus trabalhadores só podem fazer as coisas tão rápido quanto seus dispositivos móveis permitem, e muitas coisas podem desacelerar dispositivos mais antigos (e seus usuários). A capacidade de processamento e a memória de um dispositivo estão entre elas. Dispositivos mais novos sempre oferecerão capacidades de processamento mais rápidas e mais memória, o que se traduz em melhor desempenho de aplicativos e capacidades de multitarefa. Isso, claro, pode aumentar a produtividade. Agora, eu não recomendaria atualizar um dispositivo apenas por esse motivo, ou seja, você não precisa necessariamente atualizar todos os anos quando um novo dispositivo é lançado apenas por esse motivo. Mas se você tem um dispositivo mais antigo em uso há 3-5 anos, as melhorias de processamento e memória que você verá serão bastante significativas. Outra coisa que tende a avançar muito em 3-5 anos é a conectividade wireless, tanto em termos de velocidade quanto de estabilidade da conexão. Há tantos novos recursos disponíveis para tornar a transição entre redes celulares privadas e públicas, e redes celulares e Wi-Fi, perfeita. Agora há uma capacidade de identificação e alternância de rede automatizada baseada em políticas de segurança e desempenho que é muito impressionante (– e benéfica para seus trabalhadores). Claro, as tecnologias Wi-Fi 6 e 5G oferecem mais largura de banda para acesso mais rápido aos dados e aplicativos baseados na nuvem, o que está se tornando a norma. E novos dispositivos estão começando a oferecer conectividade a redes 4G/5G privadas como um recurso padrão, o que lhe dá mais alcance de cobertura wireless em áreas onde as redes Wi-Fi e celulares públicas não estão disponíveis, como pátios, portos ou espaços de eventos abertos. Eu sei que posso parecer um disco arranhado, mas você não pode ter acesso a essas velocidades aumentadas e feeds aprimorados sem migrar para um novo dispositivo que já tenha antenas wireless e componentes de computação compatíveis integrados. Estes não estão disponíveis como atualizações pós-venda. 4. A necessidade de encontrar melhores maneiras de trabalhar – À medida que as demandas dos clientes e as pressões competitivas aumentam, sua equipe precisa encontrar maneiras de fazer mais em menos tempo sem cometer erros. Você também deve encontrar maneiras de ajudar seus clientes a obter o que precisam mais rápido e com menos atrito, seja isso mantimentos, atendimento médico ou suporte em emergências. Isso significa que você precisa encontrar novas maneiras de utilizar a tecnologia móvel para capturar e compartilhar informações, impulsionar decisões e ações e facilitar interações sem atrito entre todos na sua cadeia de valor, incluindo clientes, parceiros e funcionários. Há muitos novos casos de uso e propostas de valor da tecnologia móvel, mas quase todos exigem que você faça a transição para dispositivos que já possuam um sistema operacional, um chipset e um conjunto de recursos mais modernos. Por exemplo, é possível substituir terminais de ponto de venda dedicados por um computador móvel que possa aceitar pagamentos no dispositivo e gerar um recibo em uma impressora móvel usada no quadril de um atendente de loja. No entanto, esse software de processamento de pagamento móvel e a tecnologia de deslize/tocar de pagamento relacionada não podem ser adicionados retroativamente a dispositivos mais antigos. Você terá que fazer um upgrade para aproveitar seus muitos benefícios. O mesmo vale se você quiser: - Substituir estações de trabalho fixas por computadores de mesa com uma solução mais móvel. - Substituir a medição manual de pacotes com medição móvel. - Remover a necessidade de um PIN complicado para autenticar em dispositivos móveis compartilhados. - Reduzir o número de dispositivos móveis que sua organização perde (e deve substituir) a cada ano. – Simplificar sua frota de dispositivos e padronizar em um único modelo de dispositivo que pode ser usado para vários casos de uso/papéis. – Obter acesso a aplicativos de software empresarial baseados em nuvem, como configuração simples de dispositivo e ferramentas de design de aplicativos. – Aproveitar a IA para orientar os trabalhadores, informar suas decisões ou até mesmo analisar o desempenho do negócio na borda de suas operações. Muitos modelos de IA, especialmente IA generativa/modelos de linguagem grandes projetados para funcionar “offline”, só funcionarão em dispositivos com chipsets compatíveis devido às capacidades de processamento necessárias. Eu poderia continuar e continuar com razões pelas quais é tão arriscado depender de dispositivos mais antigos para conduzir negócios. Meu ponto é: É fácil pensar que esperar "um pouco mais" para atualizar seus dispositivos móveis vai economizar dinheiro. Mas usar dispositivos que não são mais suportados do ponto de vista de segurança ou aplicativo ou que não podem se conectar à tecnologia wireless mais recente vai custar mais a longo prazo. Você terá que gastar muito tempo tentando resolver as muitas vulnerabilidades que esses dispositivos mais antigos introduzem em seu negócio. Você provavelmente terá perdas de produtividade, além de um aumento de reclamações relacionadas ao SLA, violações de conformidade de segurança/privacidade, e você estará por conta própria para resolver as coisas, porque o suporte do fabricante e do provedor do sistema operacional terminou. Portanto, não espere até o último minuto (ou até depois de perder o suporte) para renovar sua frota de dispositivos móveis. Dedique tempo agora à pesquisa de mercado para entender quais dispositivos lhe darão vários anos a mais de segurança, desempenho e suporte com base nos casos de uso projetados para esses dispositivos móveis. O tempo que sua equipe gasta agora com desenvolvimento de software, configurações de dispositivos, implantações de usuários finais e treinamento será muito menor do que o que eles gastarão tentando manter dispositivos móveis mais antigos em funcionamento após o suporte do fabricante expirar. title: Androgenetic Alopecia: A Complete Dermatology Guide
summary: Androgenetic alopecia is the most common cause of hair loss in men and women. Learn how DHT shrinks follicles, how finasteride and minoxidil work, and what to expect from treatment.
body_text: Back to blog Androgenetic Alopecia: A Complete Dermatology Guide Androgenetic alopecia is the most common cause of hair loss in both men and women, yet it's frequently mismanaged: wrong treatment, too early a quit, or no treatment at all. This guide covers what's happening at the follicle level, how diagnosis works, and how to build a treatment plan that actually holds. Dr. Dennis Porto Jul 22, 2026 · 27 min read Androgenetic alopecia is the most common cause of hair loss in men and women, and it's also one of the most mismanaged. Not because the treatments don't work. They do. But most people either start the wrong thing, quit too early, or never start at all because they got scared by something they read online. The condition itself is straightforward once you understand what's actually happening at the follicle level. The decisions that matter, like oral versus topical finasteride, when to add minoxidil, how to read your own progress, are where most people get lost. This is the complete picture. Start a chat with Dr. Dennis Porto Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. The short version Androgenetic alopecia is progressive hair thinning caused by a hormone called DHT (dihydrotestosterone), which shrinks hair follicles over time until they stop producing visible hair. It affects roughly 50% of men by age 50 and a significant number of women, particularly after menopause. The condition is genetic. If your parents or grandparents had it, your odds go up considerably. The standard diagnostic approach is a clinical history plus a close look at the scalp, often with a dermatoscope. Labs are sometimes helpful to rule out other causes of thinning (thyroid issues, iron deficiency, nutritional gaps), but the pattern of loss itself is usually diagnostic. First-line treatment for most men is finasteride (oral, 1 mg daily) to block DHT at its source, often combined with minoxidil to stimulate regrowth. For women, the options shift. Finasteride is used differently and typically only after menopause. Visible improvement takes time: you're looking at 6 to 12 months of consistent treatment before the results become hard to miss. The condition doesn't go away, but with the right plan it's very manageable. Table of contents What it actually is Who gets it (and why it's so often missed) The signs and symptoms, and what they're often confused with How it's diagnosed Treatment landscape What treatment actually feels like, week to week Side effects, monitoring, and how the plan adjusts Lifestyle and self-management: what moves the needle and what doesn't Complications and what to watch for When to seek care vs. wait it out The honest take Frequently asked questions What it actually is Androgenetic alopecia is hair loss driven by your genetics and your hormones working together. The hormone that does the damage is DHT, dihydrotestosterone. DHT is a byproduct of testosterone. An enzyme called 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone into DHT, and DHT then binds to receptors on hair follicles that are genetically sensitive to it. When DHT binds to those receptors, it gradually shrinks the follicle. The hair it produces gets thinner, shorter, and lighter with each growth cycle. Over time, the follicle miniaturizes to the point where it produces hair so fine you can't see it, or it stops producing hair altogether. That process is called follicular miniaturization, and it's the hallmark of androgenetic alopecia. Not every follicle on your scalp is equally sensitive to DHT. The follicles at your temples, your crown, and across the top of your scalp tend to have more DHT receptors. The follicles along the sides and back of your head are usually resistant. That's why the classic pattern is thinning on top with preservation around the sides, the "horseshoe" pattern in advanced cases. The follicles aren't dying because of something you did wrong. They're responding to a hormone they were genetically programmed to respond to. This also explains why finasteride works: if you block the enzyme that converts testosterone into DHT, you reduce the amount of DHT reaching those sensitive follicles. Less DHT means less miniaturization, which means the follicles can recover, at least partially, and start producing thicker, more visible hair again. Who gets it (and why it's so often missed) Androgenetic alopecia is extremely common. Roughly 50% of men show some degree of it by age 50, and it can start as early as the late teens or early twenties [per a 2014 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology ]. In women, the prevalence increases significantly after menopause, though it can begin earlier, particularly in women with a family history or underlying hormonal conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The reason it gets missed, or more accurately, the reason people don't act on it, is that the early stages are subtle. You're not waking up to clumps of hair on your pillow. What's happening is a slow, gradual decrease in hair density that you might not notice for months or even years. The hair at your temples recedes slightly. The part in your hair looks a little wider. Your ponytail feels thinner. By the time most people think "I should probably do something about this," they've already lost a meaningful amount of density. The other pattern I see constantly in practice: patients who've been told their hair loss is "just stress" or "just from a bad diet." Telogen effluvium, stress-related shedding, is real, and it does cause hair loss. But it looks different from androgenetic alopecia, and the treatments are different. Telogen effluvium causes diffuse shedding all over the scalp and is usually triggered by a specific event (illness, surgery, crash diet, major life stress). Androgenetic alopecia follows a pattern: temples, crown, midline. It progresses over years, not weeks. When a patient comes in convinced their thinning is stress-related but the pattern tells me it's androgenetic, the treatment plan changes completely. Women get misdiagnosed more often than men. Female-pattern hair loss doesn't always follow the classic male pattern. Women tend to thin diffusely across the top of the scalp while maintaining their frontal hairline, which can look a lot like telogen effluvium or iron-deficiency-related thinning. Getting the diagnosis right matters because the treatments are different for each of those conditions. The signs and symptoms, and what they're often confused with Gradual thinning at the temples and crown. This is the classic presentation in men. It starts with the hairline receding at the temples and thinning at the vertex (the crown). Early on, it can be confused with a naturally maturing hairline, which is a real thing and not the same as androgenetic alopecia. The difference is progression: a maturing hairline stabilizes, while androgenetic alopecia keeps going. Widening part line. More common in women. The part gradually widens as the hair density across the top of the scalp decreases. This gets confused with telogen effluvium or thyroid-related hair loss. The distinguishing feature is the pattern: androgenetic alopecia preserves the frontal hairline in women while thinning the midline and crown. Telogen effluvium thins everywhere, including the sides. Increased shedding. Many patients notice more hair in the shower drain or on their pillow. On its own, shedding isn't diagnostic. Everyone sheds 50 to 100 hairs a day normally. But increased shedding combined with visible thinning in a patterned distribution points toward androgenetic alopecia. When the shedding is sudden and dramatic (hundreds of hairs a day), telogen effluvium is more likely. Finer hair texture over time. The hair that grows back in affected areas is thinner, shorter, and less pigmented than it used to be. This is the miniaturization process in action. Patients often describe it as their hair feeling "wispy" or "see-through." This gets confused with aging-related hair changes, which are real but don't follow the same patterned distribution. Scalp visibility through the hair. In more advanced cases, the scalp becomes visible through the hair, especially in bright light or when the hair is wet. This is when most patients seek help, and it's often later than ideal, because the earlier you start treatment, the more follicles you have to work with. How it's diagnosed Diagnosing androgenetic alopecia is primarily clinical, meaning the pattern of loss, your history, and a close examination of the scalp usually tell the story. The first step is a detailed history. When did you first notice thinning? Is it getting worse gradually or did it happen suddenly? Any family history of hair loss? Any recent major stressors, illnesses, surgeries, or medication changes? Are you on any new supplements? For women: any changes in your menstrual cycle, new hormonal symptoms, or recent pregnancy? These questions narrow the differential quickly. The second step is examining the scalp. With a dermatoscope, a magnifying instrument with special lighting, I can see follicular miniaturization directly. I'm looking for variation in hair shaft diameter across the scalp: a mix of thick terminal hairs and thin, miniaturized hairs in the affected areas is the hallmark of androgenetic alopecia. I'm also looking at the pattern of involvement. Temples, crown, and midline versus diffuse thinning everywhere. Labs are sometimes useful, particularly to rule out other contributors. A thyroid panel (TSH, free T4), ferritin, CBC, and sometimes a hormonal panel (DHEA-S, testosterone, in women) can identify conditions that either mimic androgenetic alopecia or compound it. These are standard outpatient labs, orderable through a chat consultation and interpreted alongside your history and photos. For the vast majority of presentations, a biopsy isn't needed. The clinical picture is clear enough. If the pattern is atypical, if it doesn't fit neatly into androgenetic alopecia or any other recognizable pattern, a scalp biopsy can distinguish between different types of alopecia (scarring versus non-scarring, for example). That's the scenario where I'd recommend in-person evaluation. But in most cases, we can diagnose and start treatment through chat based on your history, photos, and labs, and use how you respond to treatment to confirm the working diagnosis. Start a chat with Dr. Dennis Porto Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. Treatment landscape Treatment for androgenetic alopecia falls into a few tiers, and the right combination depends on where you are in the process, what you're comfortable with, and what your goals are. First-line: finasteride. For men, oral finasteride 1 mg daily is the gold standard. It blocks the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) that converts testosterone to DHT, reducing DHT levels systemically. That means every follicle on your scalp benefits, not just the ones you can see thinning. I personally favor oral finasteride over topical for most patients because it's more effective, easier to stick with, and treats the entire scalp rather than just the areas you apply it to. Topical finasteride is a reasonable option for patients who are very concerned about side effects, but the tradeoff is somewhat lower efficacy and the hassle of daily application. Different dermatologists weigh that tradeoff differently, and that's a legitimate clinical choice. The evidence supports both routes. First-line adjunct: minoxidil. Minoxidil (topical or oral) stimulates hair growth through a different mechanism. It increases blood flow to the follicle and extends the growth phase of the hair cycle. It doesn't address DHT directly, so it works best in combination with finasteride rather than alone. Topical minoxidil (5% for men, 2% or 5% for women) is the over-the-counter option. Low-dose oral minoxidil is gaining traction as an alternative for patients who find the topical version messy or irritating. Second-line: combination and escalation. For patients who don't respond adequately to finasteride plus minoxidil, options include increasing finasteride dose (under supervision), adding low-dose oral minoxidil if they were only on topical, or considering platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections, which require in-person visits. Dutasteride, a more potent 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, is sometimes used off-label for hair loss when finasteride alone isn't enough. I'll flag that as off-label when I prescribe it, and I explain why I think it's defensible for that patient's situation. Adjunct: prescription-strength shampoos. Ketoconazole shampoo has mild anti-androgenic properties at the scalp level and can help with seborrheic dermatitis, which often coexists with androgenetic alopecia and can contribute to shedding. For women: the treatment landscape shifts. Finasteride is used at different doses and typically only after menopause due to teratogenicity risks. Spironolactone (an anti-androgen) is often the first-line hormonal option for premenopausal women. Topical minoxidil remains a mainstay. I have no incentive to push one medication over another. The consultation is what I charge for, so the recommendation reflects what fits your situation, not a formulary. What treatment actually feels like, week to week This is the part most articles skip, and it's the part that matters most for whether you actually stick with treatment. Weeks 1 to 4: You start the medication. Nothing visible happens. Some patients on minoxidil notice increased shedding in the first few weeks. This is the "minoxidil shed," and it's actually a good sign. It means the medication is pushing older, miniaturized hairs out of the follicle to make room for new growth. It's alarming if you don't know to expect it. Months 1 to 3: Still nothing visible to the naked eye. With a dermatoscope, I can sometimes see early signs: fine vellus hairs forming in previously bare areas, slight changes in hair shaft diameter. But you won't see this in the mirror. This is the window where most people quit, and it's the worst time to quit. Months 3 to 6: Shedding typically stabilizes. Some patients start noticing that their hair feels slightly thicker, or that they're losing less hair in the shower. Photos taken in the same lighting may start showing subtle differences. This is the "is it working?" phase, and the honest answer is usually "yes, but you need more time." Months 6 to 12: This is when the results become visible. Hair density improves, thin areas fill in, and the overall quality of the hair (thickness, texture, coverage) gets noticeably better. Month 12 is really when patients look at their before-and-after photos and see meaningful change. Beyond 12 months: Maintenance. The gains you've made hold as long as you stay on treatment. If you stop finasteride, DHT levels return to baseline and the miniaturization process resumes. This is a long-term commitment. On FutureClinic, that trajectory isn't a one-shot conversation. Your same doctor is in the chat as you experience it, so adjustments happen as the response unfolds, not at the next six-month visit. Side effects, monitoring, and how the plan adjusts The side effect conversation around finasteride is the most overblown topic in hair loss. The side effects are real. They're also rare, and they're manageable. Sexual side effects (oral finasteride). The most discussed concern is changes in libido, erectile function, or ejaculate volume. In clinical trials, these side effects occurred in roughly 2 to 4% of men taking finasteride 1 mg daily, which means 96 to 98% of men experienced no sexual side effects at all [per the original Merck trials and subsequent meta-analyses]. When side effects do occur, they're usually mild and often resolve either with continued use or after stopping the medication. What I tell patients: libido and erectile quality vary day to day. That's normal physiology. Once you start a medication you're anxious about, you become hyper-aware of every fluctuation. It's genuinely hard to separate "the medication is doing this" from "I'm monitoring myself so closely that I'm noticing normal variation I never paid attention to before." Having a doctor who knows these medications well and can walk you through that distinction honestly makes a real difference. Topical finasteride and side effects. Topical finasteride does reduce systemic DHT exposure compared to oral, which is why the side effect profile is somewhat better. But "somewhat" is the key word. There is still systemic absorption with topical finasteride. It's not a perfectly local treatment. The idea that topical finasteride is "side-effect-free" is marketing, not medicine. Minoxidil side effects. Topical minoxidil can cause scalp irritation, dryness, or flaking, usually from the propylene glycol in the solution, not the minoxidil itself. Switching to a foam formulation often fixes this. Oral minoxidil at low doses can cause fluid retention, slight drops in blood pressure, or increased body hair (hypertrichosis). These are dose-dependent and manageable. Monitoring. For oral finasteride, no routine blood work is typically needed. The medication is well-studied and the safety profile is established. For oral minoxidil, I'll sometimes check blood pressure and watch for signs of fluid retention, especially in patients with cardiovascular history. For women on spironolactone, periodic potassium levels are standard. Adjusting the plan. If a patient reports side effects, the first step is an honest conversation about whether what they're experiencing is likely medication-related or coincidental. If it's genuinely medication-related, we adjust: reduce the dose, switch the route (oral to topical or vice versa), or try a different medication altogether. The plan isn't set in stone. It evolves based on how you respond. Lifestyle and self-management: what moves the needle and what doesn't I'm going to be direct about this: the lifestyle factors that move the needle for androgenetic alopecia are fewer than most articles suggest. What actually matters: Manage coexisting scalp conditions. Seborrheic dermatitis and dandruff are common in patients with androgenetic alopecia, and untreated scalp inflammation can contribute to shedding. A prescription-strength ketoconazole shampoo used 2 to 3 times a week addresses both the fungal component and has mild anti-androgenic effects at the scalp. Most people overlook this because they think of dandruff and hair loss as separate problems. They're often connected. Manage stress and sleep. Chronic stress and poor sleep can trigger telogen effluvium, a type of diffuse shedding that stacks on top of the androgenetic thinning you're already dealing with. This isn't a wellness platitude. Telogen effluvium from sustained stress is a real, measurable phenomenon, and it compounds the visual impact of androgenetic alopecia. Avoid crash diets and dramatic caloric shifts. Sudden, severe caloric restriction is one of the most reliable triggers for telogen effluvium. If you're going to change your diet or ramp up your training, do it gradually. The metabolic shock of a crash diet can cause a wave of shedding 2 to 3 months later. What doesn't matter as much as the internet suggests: Specific supplements (biotin, saw palmetto, collagen). Biotin deficiency can cause hair loss, but actual biotin deficiency is rare in people eating a normal diet. Supplementing biotin when you're not deficient doesn't improve hair. Saw palmetto has weak evidence as a DHT blocker, nowhere near the efficacy of finasteride. Collagen supplements have no meaningful evidence for androgenetic alopecia. Special shampoos (outside ketoconazole). "Hair growth" shampoos without active pharmaceutical ingredients are marketing. A gentle, non-stripping shampoo is fine. You don't need a $40 bottle with caffeine and biotin in it. Scalp massages. There's a small body of evidence suggesting scalp massage may increase hair thickness, but the effect size is tiny compared to finasteride or minoxidil. It's not harmful, but it's not a treatment. Start a chat with Dr. Dennis Porto Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. Complications and what to watch for Androgenetic alopecia isn't medically dangerous. It doesn't cause pain, it doesn't affect organ function, and it doesn't progress to anything life-threatening. But the psychological impact is real and worth naming honestly. Patients who delay treatment, especially younger patients who notice thinning in their twenties, often end up in a worse position than they needed to be. The follicles that have fully miniaturized are much harder to recover than follicles that are still in the early stages of thinning. Starting treatment when you first notice a problem gives you the most follicles to work with. Waiting two or three years means some of those follicles may be past the point where medication alone can bring them back. The other complication I see is treatment discontinuation. Patients start finasteride, see improvement at month 8 or 10, feel good about their hair, and stop the medication, either because they think they're "cured" or because they get nervous about long-term use. Within 6 to 12 months of stopping, the miniaturization process resumes and the gains reverse. This isn't a course of antibiotics. It's a maintenance medication. Understanding that upfront saves a lot of frustration. For women, untreated androgenetic alopecia can progress to the point where the scalp is clearly visible through the hair across the entire top of the head. This is harder to reverse than early-stage thinning, and the treatment options for women are narrower than for men. When to seek care vs. wait it out Emergencies first. Androgenetic alopecia itself doesn't have emergent presentations. But sudden, rapid hair loss (large clumps coming out over days, circular bald patches appearing overnight, hair loss accompanied by scalp pain, burning, or scarring) is not androgenetic alopecia. These presentations can indicate alopecia areata, scarring alopecia, or other conditions that need prompt evaluation. If you notice sudden patchy hair loss with scarring or skin changes on the scalp, see a doctor promptly. If there are signs of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, joint pain alongside hair changes), that warrants urgent medical attention. The middle tier: this is what the chat is for. If you've noticed gradual thinning that's been progressing over months or years, if your hairline is receding or your part is widening, if you've tried over-the-counter minoxidil and aren't sure if it's enough, this is exactly the kind of presentation that a chat consultation handles well. I can review your photos, take a detailed history, order labs if needed to rule out other contributors, and build a treatment plan that fits your situation. Most people in this category delay care because of cost, scheduling, or the assumption that hair loss isn't "serious enough" to warrant a doctor's time. It absolutely is. And self-treating with supplements or over-the-counter products alone often fails because the diagnosis was incomplete. Maybe there's an iron deficiency contributing, or a thyroid issue, or the thinning pattern calls for a prescription medication that over-the-counter options can't replace. A real consultation with a real doctor: diagnoses, prescriptions, labs, just through chat, between you and a doctor. Same medicine, same depth, same doctor staying with you. What's different is that you start it from your phone whenever you're ready, and most replies come back the same day. You can either keep researching finasteride on Reddit threads and supplement forums, or you can spend the same fifteen minutes in a chat with a board-certified dermatologist who can actually look at your photos, pull your records, order the right labs, and write the prescription if that's the right call. The "I can manage this with information" tier. If your thinning is very early and you're not ready for medication, the actionable steps are: start documenting with consistent photos (same lighting, same angle, monthly), use a ketoconazole shampoo 2 to 3 times a week, manage your stress and sleep, and avoid crash diets. If the thinning progresses despite this, that's your signal to talk to a doctor. The honest take Here's what I want you to understand about androgenetic alopecia that most content online gets wrong. The topical-versus-oral finasteride debate is framed as if topical is the "safe" version and oral is the "risky" version. That framing is incomplete. Topical finasteride does reduce systemic DHT exposure, but there's still systemic absorption. You're not eliminating the possibility of side effects. You're reducing it somewhat. Meanwhile, you're also reducing efficacy and adding the hassle of a messy daily application with variable compounding quality depending on the pharmacy. I used to recommend topical finasteride more confidently as a way to get the benefits with fewer risks. My thinking has shifted. In practice, oral finasteride just produces better results, not only because patients stick with a pill more reliably, but because it improves hair quality across the entire scalp, not just the spots where you'd be applying a topical. The side effect fear is the other thing I'd push back on. There is way too much fixation online on finasteride side effects. The side effects are real. I'm not dismissing them. But they occur in a small minority of patients, they're usually mild, and they're manageable. What's unfortunate is how many people are missing out on treatment that would genuinely help them because they've become paralyzed by stories they read online. The volume and intensity of the fear is disproportionate to the actual incidence. Patients would be much better served working closely with their dermatologist, having someone who can coach them through the early months, help them distinguish normal variation from actual side effects, and adjust the treatment if something genuinely isn't right. Consistency is the most important part of improvement, and it's entirely under your control. The patients who do well are the ones who start treatment, stick with it through the months where nothing seems to be happening, and trust the process. The patients who struggle are the ones who start and stop, switch medications every few weeks, or quit at month four, right before the payoff starts. Frequently asked questions Does finasteride work for everyone? Finasteride works for the majority of men with androgenetic alopecia. In clinical studies, roughly 80 to 90% of men on finasteride 1 mg daily either maintained their hair or saw improvement over a two-year period [per long-term extension studies of the original Phase III trials]. "Not working" usually means one of two things: the patient hasn't given it enough time (visible results take 6 to 12 months), or the medication stabilized their loss without producing dramatic regrowth, which is still a clinical success, even if it doesn't feel like one. Can women take finasteride? Finasteride is used in women, but with important caveats. It's typically reserved for postmenopausal women because finasteride can cause birth defects if taken during pregnancy. The dosing is different from what's used in men. For premenopausal women, spironolactone is usually the first-line anti-androgen option. This is a conversation that needs to happen with a dermatologist who treats female hair loss regularly. What happens if I stop taking finasteride? If you stop finasteride, DHT levels return to baseline and the miniaturization process resumes. Most patients who discontinue finasteride see their hair loss progress back to where it would have been without treatment within 6 to 12 months. The gains don't persist without the medication. This is a maintenance treatment, not a cure. Is topical finasteride really safer than oral? Topical finasteride has a somewhat lower side effect profile than oral, but it's not side-effect-free. There is systemic absorption with topical application. Some of the medication gets into your bloodstream regardless. The side effect risk is reduced, not eliminated. Meanwhile, the efficacy is also somewhat lower, and the quality of compounded formulations varies significantly depending on the pharmacy. The idea that topical finasteride is a completely different safety category from oral is overstated. How do I know if my hair loss is androgenetic alopecia or something else? The pattern of loss is the biggest clue. Androgenetic alopecia follows a predictable distribution: temples, crown, and midline in men; diffuse thinning across the top with frontal hairline preservation in women. If your hair loss is sudden, patchy, or diffuse without a clear pattern, other diagnoses are more likely (telogen effluvium, alopecia areata, thyroid-related loss, iron deficiency). A dermatologist can usually distinguish these with a history, photos, dermatoscopy, and sometimes labs. This is exactly the kind of evaluation a chat consultation is built for. Send photos, walk through your history, and get a real answer for your specific pattern. Can minoxidil alone treat androgenetic alopecia? Minoxidil alone can help, but it doesn't address the root cause. Minoxidil stimulates hair growth and extends the growth phase of the hair cycle, but it doesn't block DHT. For most patients with androgenetic alopecia, using minoxidil without finasteride means you're stimulating growth while the underlying miniaturization process continues. The combination of both is more effective than either alone. Do hair growth supplements work? Most hair growth supplements have weak or no evidence for androgenetic alopecia. Biotin supplementation only helps if you're actually biotin-deficient, which is uncommon in people eating a normal diet. Saw palmetto has mild 5-alpha reductase inhibitory activity, but the effect is nowhere near finasteride. Collagen, keratin, and most "hair vitamin" blends have no rigorous evidence supporting their use for androgenetic alopecia. If you're spending money on supplements instead of proven treatments, you're likely delaying real improvement. How long do I need to take finasteride? Indefinitely, as long as you want to maintain the results. Androgenetic alopecia is a progressive condition driven by ongoing DHT exposure. Finasteride manages it by keeping DHT levels suppressed. When you stop the medication, DHT returns to baseline and the process resumes. Most patients who do well on finasteride plan to stay on it long-term. What about the "post-finasteride syndrome" I've read about online? Post-finasteride syndrome, persistent sexual or neurological side effects after stopping finasteride, is reported by some patients online, but it remains poorly understood and controversial in the medical literature. Large-scale studies have not consistently demonstrated a causal link, and the condition doesn't have a universally accepted diagnostic definition. That said, I take every patient's reported experience seriously. If someone on finasteride reports side effects, we address them: reduce the dose, switch the route, or stop the medication entirely. The important thing is having a doctor who listens, takes your concerns seriously, and adjusts the plan accordingly. Are there new treatments coming? Yes, and a couple are genuinely exciting. PP405 is a topical medication in development that targets dormant follicles through a non-hormonal mechanism, completely different from finasteride. Early results are promising, though it likely won't be widely available until after 2028. VDPH101 is a delayed-release reformulation of oral minoxidil that keeps the drug in the therapeutic range longer, potentially improving efficacy while reducing side effects like fluid retention. Both are worth watching, but neither replaces what's available and proven right now. Should I see a dermatologist for hair loss, or can my primary care doctor handle it? A board-certified dermatologist who treats hair loss regularly is the best fit for this condition. Primary care doctors can prescribe finasteride, and many do a good job with straightforward cases. But the nuances, like distinguishing androgenetic alopecia from other types of hair loss, choosing between treatment routes, monitoring response with dermatoscopy, adjusting the plan when the first approach isn't enough, are where dermatology-specific training matters. I've seen patients who weren't improving because the compounding was off, or who were on a formulation that wasn't appropriate for them, because no one with deep experience in hair loss was overseeing the treatment. Bottom line Androgenetic alopecia is common, progressive, and very treatable, but the treatment only works if you start it, stick with it, and have a doctor who knows how to adjust the plan as you go. The earlier you start, the more follicles you have to work with. Consistency is the most important part of improvement, and it's entirely under your control. If you want a personalized treatment plan for your hair loss, whether that's figuring out if finasteride is right for you, choosing between oral and topical, or building a combination approach that fits your goals, you can start a chat consultation with me through FutureClinic. It's a real medical consultation, just through chat. Same doctor, same depth, and I stay with you as the plan unfolds. Start a chat with Dr. Dennis Porto Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. This article is intended as educational information, not personal medical advice. For one-to-one guidance on your specific situation, talk to your own doctor, or start a chat consultation with a FutureClinic doctor and get a real, personalized answer for your case. title: Alight achieves Gold Hermes Award for valuable work on leave of absence communications
body_text: Alight’s leave communications prepare employees in advance of key leave milestones to improve confidence and outcomes. At the same time, the materials empower managers with clear action items, guidance and resources to support employees effectively. For both employees and managers, Alight’s leave communications materials increase awareness and understanding of leave benefits, processes and services. The program also delivers a consistent, transparent communication experience aligned to the client’s specific leave program. Key features of Alight’s leave communications include: Launch-related information with FAQs: Emails are sent to employees when a company launches Alight’s Leave Solutions offering, explaining how Alight will support them before, during and after a leave of absence. FAQs help reduce anxiety and call volume by providing answers to common employee questions about eligibility, job protection, documentation requirements, pay during leave and return-to-work expectations. Flyers, newsletters and guides: These communications contextualize leave of absence in various formats, including digestible visual references, embedded communication in employee newsletters and an overview of what employees can expect when requesting and taking a leave of absence. Manager/HR FAQs and information sessions: A more detailed FAQ set tailored to HR teams, addressing policy alignment, compliance considerations, escalation paths and how Alight integrates with existing absence programs. Additionally, HR teams receive a structured live session to answer questions about the transition, a step-by-step checklist and a quick guide on how to manage employee leave of absence and workplace accommodations. Hermes Creative Awards honor the messengers and creators of the information revolution, recognizing the creative industry’s best publications, branding collateral, websites, videos, advertising, marketing, and communication programs. This honor follows several other awards for Alight in 2026, including IAOP’s Global 100® list for the thirteenth year in a row, as well as Fortune’s Most Innovative Companies in America and NelsonHall’s NEAT assessment for Benefits Administration . Learn more about Alight’s leave of absence administration solution here .

title: MARA Signs Agreement with HIF to Acquire Strategic Powered Land Site in Texas
summary: Expands MARA's digital infrastructure platform with access to approximately 2 GW of power capacity HIF to retain minority ownership in…...
body_text: MARA Signs Agreement with HIF to Acquire Strategic Powered Land Site in Texas July 09, 2026 8:05 am EDT Download as PDF Expands MARA's digital infrastructure platform with access to approximately 2 GW of power capacity HIF to retain minority ownership in the project Thousands of jobs expected for Texas MIAMI, FL and HOUSTON, TX, July 09, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- MARA Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: MARA) (“MARA”), a leading energy and digital infrastructure company, and HIF USA LLC (“HIF”), a leading energy and sustainable fuels company, today announced that they have entered into a definitive agreement under which MARA will acquire from HIF a large-scale powered land site in Matagorda County, Texas, approximately 90 miles southwest of Houston. HIF will continue its advanced fuels development plans on other sites. The site encompasses more than 1,200 acres and is expected to provide access to up to an initial 1 GW of grid capacity by October 2027 and up to 2 GW by April 2028. The site is well positioned to support next-generation, efficient digital infrastructure development, and has already received interest from potential High-Performance Computing (“HPC”) tenants. MARA intends to develop the site through its previously announced partnership with Starwood Digital Ventures as a large-scale digital infrastructure campus capable of supporting high-performance computing workloads, as well as flexible compute operations, including Bitcoin mining. Upon execution of a lease with an HPC tenant, HIF will retain a minority ownership interest in the project. The transaction enables HIF to unlock value from infrastructure assets while maintaining participation in the site’s future development and supporting its broader advanced fuels strategy. Upon full energization, the site is expected to more than double MARA's potential power capacity to approximately 4.8 GW across its portfolio (including the anticipated close of MARA’s previously announced agreement to acquire Long Ridge Energy & Power), further strengthening MARA's position as a developer and operator of large-scale digital infrastructure. “This transaction advances our strategy of securing strategically located infrastructure assets capable of supporting high-performance compute and bitcoin workloads,” said Fred Thiel, MARA's chairman and CEO. “As demand for digital infrastructure continues to grow, we believe sites with access to reliable, scalable power will become increasingly valuable. This acquisition meaningfully expands our long-term development pipeline and strengthens our ability to support high-performance compute and maximize the value of that power over time. We look forward to working with our partners at the site to deliver on the project buildout and drive long-term value for all our stakeholders.” Renato Pereira, CEO of HIF USA, said, “We are pleased to welcome MARA to our long-term partnership with Matagorda County, accelerating our commitment to economic investment and jobs for Texans. The development of this digital infrastructure serves as a powerful economic anchor to strengthen Matagorda County and create local career opportunities for a prosperous future. We have given Notice to Proceed for construction on the switchyard to connect the site to the grid. We continue work on our advanced fuels facilities on other sites we control in Texas and worldwide to provide new sources of secure energy supply to meet rapidly growing global demand.” Site Development Details Phased construction of the digital infrastructure campus is expected to begin in 2026, contingent upon regulatory approvals. By combining MARA's expertise in securing and managing large-scale power loads, Starwood Digital Ventures' world-class experience developing and operating data centers, and HIF's history in Matagorda, MARA believes the site is well positioned to support future digital infrastructure opportunities and create long-term value for customers, local communities, and shareholders. MARA has a proven track record of investing in the communities where it operates while supporting grid reliability and local economic growth. To date, MARA has invested more than $1.2 billion in Texas. MARA intends to continue investing significantly to develop a premier digital infrastructure campus that is expected to support thousands of construction and permanent full-time jobs upon completion. About MARA MARA (NASDAQ: MARA) deploys digital energy technologies to advance the world’s energy systems. Harnessing the power of compute, MARA transforms excess energy into digital capital, balancing the grid and accelerating the deployment of critical infrastructure. Building on its expertise to redefine the future of energy, MARA develops technologies that reduce the energy demands of high-performance computing applications, from AI to the edge. About HIF Global HIF Global is a world leading e-Fuels company developing large scale infrastructure projects to recycle captured CO₂ and produce synthetic fuels for existing engines. The name HIF reflects the company’s mission: to produce Highly Innovative Fuels that contribute to global energy security. HIF already produces e-Fuels at its HIF Haru Oni facility in southern Chile and is developing large scale projects in the United States, Uruguay, Brazil, Australia, and Chile. For more information, visit www.hifglobal.com . Forward-Looking Statements This press release contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws. Such forward-looking statements include, among other things, statements related to the occurrence of any event, change or other circumstance that could give rise to the exercise of any return or forfeiture right under, the purchase agreement entered into in connection with MARA’s acquisition of the site; MARA’s planned development of the site as a digital infrastructure campus; the expected power capacity (including as a result of the agreement to acquire Long Ridge Energy & Power), scalability and performance of the site; the anticipated ability to commercialize the site’s power capacity for high-performance compute and bitcoin workloads; the number of construction and other jobs anticipated to be created; and the anticipated benefits of the transaction to MARA. title: Vertiv, a Platinum Equity Portfolio Company, to List on New York Stock Exchange Through Business Combination with GS Acquisition Holdings
summary: Vertiv, a Platinum Equity portfolio company, and a global provider of critical digital infrastructure and continuity solutions, today announced it will become a publicly traded company through a merger with GS Acquisition Holdings Corp (NYSE: GSAH, GSAH.U, GSAH WS), a special purpose acquisition company co-sponsored by an affiliate of The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. and David M. Cote.
body_text: Columbus, Ohio Dec. 10, 2019 – Vertiv Holdings LLC (“Vertiv”), a Platinum Equity portfolio company, and a global provider of critical digital infrastructure and continuity solutions, today announced it will become a publicly traded company through a merger with GS Acquisition Holdings Corp (NYSE: GSAH, GSAH.U, GSAH WS), a special purpose acquisition company co-sponsored by an affiliate of The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. and David M. Cote. Mr. Cote, CEO of GSAH and former Executive Chairman of the Board and CEO of Honeywell, will serve as Executive Chairman of Vertiv. Vertiv's existing management team will continue to be led by 30-year industry veteran CEO Rob Johnson. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2020 and at close Vertiv’s stock will trade under the ticker symbol NYSE: VRT. “Platinum Equity, Rob Johnson and his team have done a tremendous job over the last several years positioning Vertiv for long-term success. The Company is exactly the asset we were looking for, with a great position in a good industry, products differentiated by technology, strong organic and inorganic growth potential, and opportunities for sustained improvements over time. Taken together, I am delighted with the near- and long-term prospects for Vertiv and the opportunity this represents for shareowners,” said Mr. Cote. Tom Gores, Chairman and CEO, Platinum Equity, said, “I’m proud of the work our team has done at Vertiv in positioning it where it is today, and I’m very excited about the new partnership with our friend David and long-time partners at Goldman Sachs. Rob Johnson and the management team have done a tremendous job preparing the company for its next phase of growth.” “This transaction enables us to accelerate our growth and innovation strategy and broaden our opportunities as we continue to focus on the ever-evolving needs of our customers,” said Vertiv CEO Rob Johnson. “Our partnership with David, who has a proven track record of driving operational improvements and shareholder value, will further enhance our trajectory as we look to capitalize on our strong foundation in a growing industry.” Platinum Equity Partner Jacob Kotzubei, who will become a board member of the newly listed company, said, “We are pleased to partner with Goldman Sachs and Dave Cote on the next phase of Vertiv’s journey, and to participate in the company’s future success as a meaningful shareholder. We also look forward to working with Dave, Rob and the Vertiv management team to accelerate Vertiv’s product and service leadership in the industry.” With operations in more than 130 countries, Vertiv is a global leader in delivering the hardware, software, analytics and ongoing services customers rely on to enable their vital applications to run continuously, perform optimally and grow with their business needs. The company’s portfolio of power, thermal and IT management along with cooling and IT infrastructure solutions and services that extend from the cloud to the edge of the network, generated nearly $4.3 billion in revenue in 2018. Key Transaction Terms The transaction, unanimously approved by both boards of directors, is expected to close in the first quarter of 2020, subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals, and approval of GSAH’s stockholders. At closing, the public company’s name will be changed to Vertiv Holdings Co. Upon closing, Vertiv will have an anticipated pro forma enterprise value of approximately $5.3 billion, or 8.9x the company’s estimated 2020 pro forma Adjusted EBITDA of approximately $595 million. Upon completion, it is expected that, subject to various purchase price adjustments and any redemptions by the public stockholders of GSAH, Platinum Equity will hold approximately 38% of Vertiv Holdings Co and the sponsor (including Mr. Cote and affiliates of The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.) will own approximately 5% of Vertiv Holdings Co. In addition to the approximately $705 million of cash held in GSAH’s trust account, additional investors (including affiliates of Mr. Cote and affiliates of The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.) have committed to participate in the transaction through a $1.239 billion private placement. After giving effect to any redemptions by the public stockholders of GSAH, the balance of the approximately $705 million in cash held in GSAH’s trust account, together with the $1.239 billion in private placement proceeds, will be used to pay $415 million cash consideration (subject to certain adjustments) to Vertiv stockholders, pay transaction expenses and reduce Vertiv’s existing indebtedness to up to 3.6x 2019 estimated pro forma Adjusted EBITDA. The remainder of the consideration payable to the stockholders of Vertiv will consist of shares of GSAH common stock. The transaction will be effected pursuant to the Agreement and Plan of Merger (“the Merger Agreement”), entered into by and among GSAH, Vertiv Holdings, LLC, VPE Holdings, LLC (Vertiv Holdings, LLC’s parent), and the other parties thereto. Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC acted as lead placement agent and exclusive financial advisor to GSAH. J.P. Morgan Securities LLC acted as financial advisor to Vertiv. Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP acted as legal advisor to GSAH. Morgan, Lewis & Bockius, LLP and Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP acted as joint legal advisors to Platinum Equity and Vertiv. Conference Call Information Investors may listen to a presentation regarding the proposed transaction on Tuesday, December 10, 2019 starting at 10:30 a.m. ET. The call can be accessed by dialing 1-877-883-0383 (domestic toll-free number) or 1-412-902-6506 (international) and providing the conference ID: 8567556, or asking for the GSAH-Vertiv transaction announcement call. The live webcast of the investor call as well as related presentation materials will be available at https://www.gsacquisition.com/ . A replay of the teleconference and webcast will also be available for approximately 30 days at https://www.gsacquisition.com/ . About Vertiv Vertiv brings together hardware, software, analytics and ongoing services to ensure its customers’ vital applications run continuously, perform optimally and grow with their business needs. Vertiv solves the most important challenges facing today’s data centers, communication networks and commercial and industrial facilities with a portfolio of power, cooling and IT infrastructure solutions and services that extends from the cloud to the edge of the network. Headquartered in Columbus, Ohio, Vertiv employs around 20,000 people and does business in more than 130 countries. For more information, and for the latest news and content from Vertiv, visit Vertiv.com . About GSAH GS Acquisition Holdings Corp (NYSE: GSAH) is a special purpose acquisition company formed for the purpose of effecting merger, stock purchase or similar business combination with one or more businesses. The company is sponsored by an affiliate of The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. and David M. Cote. In June 2018, GSAH completed its initial public offering, raising $690 million from investors. About Platinum Equity Founded in 1995 by Tom Gores, Platinum Equity is a global investment firm with more than $19 billion of assets under management and a portfolio of approximately 40 operating companies that serve customers around the world. Platinum Equity specializes in mergers, acquisitions and operations – a trademarked strategy it calls M&A&O® – acquiring and operating companies in a broad range of business markets, including manufacturing, distribution, transportation and logistics, equipment rental, metals services, media and entertainment, technology, telecommunications and other industries.
